lead: Hops extract is a concentrate of the cone-shaped flowers of the female Humulus lupulus plant, the same ingredient that gives beer its bitterness. It is sold in capsules, teas and sleep-and-relaxation blends, frequently paired with valerian, chamomile or passionflower.[1][2]

In a looks context, hops sits in the recovery category: people who take it do so hoping to fall asleep more easily and rest more deeply, and sleep is the stage at which skin, hair, muscle and body composition recover. Better rest is associated with a fresher face, steadier training and more consistent routines, so a calming herb is a small link in a longer chain toward appearance.

The cones carry lupulin glands rich in alpha and beta acids, essential oils and polyphenols such as xanthohumol and the phytoestrogen 8-prenylnaringenin.[1][2] Human research on hops includes small trials of hop-valerian combinations for occasional insomnia, menopause-symptom studies, and metabolic and pharmacokinetic work; reviews describe the data for several uses as still limited.[11][7]

chain: Hops extract taken as a calming supplement
Easier sleep onset and more restful nights, as users hope
More recovery for skin, hair and muscle
Fresher look and more consistent training
angle.text: People use hops extract at night, usually in blends, to wind down and sleep better. Sleep quality is tied to how rested the face looks and how well training and recovery go, which is the route by which a sleep herb is connected to appearance.

paras: Humulus lupulus is a perennial climbing bine in the Cannabaceae family, the family that also holds cannabis. It is native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere and is grown commercially in places such as Germany's Hallertau, the US Pacific Northwest and the Czech Republic.[1] Only the female plants produce the cones used in brewing and herbal products.[1][2]

The cones contain lupulin glands that secrete resins. Grokipedia gives the resin share as roughly 15 to 35 percent alpha acids, with beta acids, essential oils and polyphenols making up the rest of the active fraction.[1] In supplements, the cones are dried and extracted into standardised powders or liquid extracts; in teas and pillows, the dried cones are used more directly.[2]

Hops have a long record in brewing. Wikipedia places the first documented use of hops in beer in the 9th century, and the earliest documented hop cultivation in 736 in the Hallertau region of Germany; hop gardens are also mentioned in the will of Pepin the Short in 768.[2] The abbess Hildegard of Bingen, writing roughly three centuries later, is often cited as an early written source on hopped beer.[2]

Hopped beer spread gradually. The first mention of hops in German brewing dates to 1079, and in the early 16th century some Protestants favoured hopped beer partly because hops, unlike the herb blend gruit, were not taxed by the Church.[2] Hopped beer reached England from Holland around 1400, and hops were first grown in Kent in 1524 by Dutch farmers; cultivation in the United States began in 1629.[2] Today the United States and Germany together account for about three quarters of world production, at roughly 47,500 and 46,900 tonnes respectively in 2020.[2]

Alongside its brewing role, the plant has a folk-medicine history as a sedative, and the hop-filled pillow is a traditional remedy for sleeplessness.[2] Modern supplement makers drew on that tradition when they began selling standardised hop extracts for evening relaxation, usually blended with valerian.[2][11]

The female cone contains lupulin glands that secrete resins and essential oils. The alpha acids (humulones) are the compounds that turn into bitter iso-alpha acids when hops are boiled in wort, while the beta acids (lupulones) contribute aroma and are less bitter.[2] Xanthohumol is the principal prenylated flavonoid of the plant, and 8-prenylnaringenin, a minor constituent, is described as one of the most potent phytoestrogens known.[2]

Supplement extracts differ in which fraction they emphasise. Some are standardised to bitter acids, others to flavonoids, and combination sleep products pair a hops extract with valerian root; the tested valerian-hops extract Ze 91019 is one such defined combination.[11] This variety is one reason that results from one preparation are not automatically applied to another in the research literature.

Stuffing dried hops into pillows is a long-standing folk remedy for sleeplessness, and herbal medicine has used hops for anxiety, restlessness and insomnia in the manner of valerian.[2] Modern products usually combine hops with valerian or other calming herbs and are taken in the evening.[2][11]

Hops appear in herbal teas, soft drinks and beer, and a hops-derived supplement is marketed for appetite control.[2] Hop extracts also appear in some cosmetic formulations, and a 2024 safety assessment in the International Journal of Toxicology reviewed hops as a cosmetic ingredient.[13] A 2023 review of natural compounds for hair loss lists botanical candidates among many plants.[14]

Reference texts attribute the calming action of hops to resin acids such as humulone and lupulone, which are described as acting on GABA-A receptors, though the mechanism is described as inferred from laboratory and animal work.[1] 8-Prenylnaringenin is described as one of the most potent phytoestrogens known, which is why hops have been studied for menopause-related symptoms.[2]

Xanthohumol, a prenylated chalcone, has been studied separately for anti-inflammatory activity. In a placebo-controlled, single-blinded crossover study of 14 healthy adults, a beverage with a very low xanthohumol amount was followed by a smaller inflammatory response in blood cells stimulated in the lab with lipoteichoic acid.[8]

Reviews of herbal products for sleep and for women's health describe the human evidence for hops as limited, with no single condition strongly established.[2] A 2021 review of herbs used in menopause concluded that available data did not fully support hops for menopausal symptoms, while naming black cohosh and red clover as more consistently helpful.[7]

A 2025 randomised controlled feasibility trial in Brain and Behavior examined a valerian-hops combination (Ze 91019) for sleep duration and daytime cognition and mood in occasional insomnia.[11] Randomised trials have also looked at hops for early menopausal symptoms and hot flashes (2016) and postmenopausal sexual dysfunction in 63 women (2023).[12][9] A randomised crossover trial in healthy-weight men tested a hops extract on gut hormone secretion and energy intake.[10]

Registered studies include an acute cognition and mood study in 150 healthy participants, a 443-participant menopause-symptom supplement trial, and pharmacokinetic studies of hop prenylflavonoids and botanical supplements.[3][4][5][6] No studies of hops extract for appearance outcomes were found.

Hops are generally considered safe in food and traditional use. Harvesting the cones can cause contact dermatitis in a small share of workers, and hops are toxic to dogs.[2] Because 8-prenylnaringenin is estrogenic, reviews of botanicals for women's health discuss hop products alongside other phytoestrogen herbs.[7][2]
Hops combined with other sedative herbs may add to drowsiness, and product labels for combination herbal products typically advise asking a doctor before use if taking other medications.[2]

Hops extract is sold as an over-the-counter dietary supplement in most markets and is also found in multi-herb sleep and relaxation formulas, herbal teas and some soft drinks.[2] Online sleep and recovery discussions mention it mostly as one ingredient in nighttime stacks rather than as a stand-alone product, usually alongside magnesium, valerian, chamomile or passionflower. Discussion tied specifically to appearance is sparse; people who raise it tend to frame it as part of a wind-down routine meant to improve sleep quality, which in turn is associated with how rested the face looks and how well training recovery goes.

Hops also appear in skincare. A 2024 International Journal of Toxicology safety assessment reviewed hop-derived ingredients as used in cosmetics, covering their use in formulations that draw on the plant's flavonoids and resin acids.[13] Beer drinkers encounter hops in a different way, as the bitterness and aroma component of the finished drink, which is a distinct exposure from concentrated supplement extracts.

name: Hops extract

card.summary: Beer-flavoring flower sold in sleep supplements; human sedative evidence is limited and appearance use is unstudied.

quick.overview:
Hops are the flowers used in brewing, and extracts are sold for sleep and relaxation, often in blends.
Reference pages say human evidence for a sedative effect is limited. No appearance use has been studied.
quick.mechanism: Resin acids and flavonoids such as xanthohumol are the key compounds; one, 8-prenylnaringenin, is a potent phytoestrogen. How hops might affect sleep is not established.
quick.risks: Hops are generally considered safe; contact dermatitis is reported in harvest workers. The phytoestrogen content is of research interest.
